description: HTTP request and response vectors. Spec: docs/protocol.md, "Pairing", "Files: phone -> PC", "Files: PC -> phone" and "Error codes". The device IDs are test keys 1 (PC), 2 (phone, paired) and 3 (not paired) from device-id.json.
howToRead: Each exchange has a context (the PC-side state the response depends on), a request and a response. context.client.deviceId is the device ID derived from the TLS client certificate (always present: a client certificate is mandatory in the TLS handshake, so a missing certificate never reaches HTTP, see tls[]); context.client.paired says whether it is in devices. body is a JSON value (or a raw string when it is not JSON). bodyBytes is a binary body of that many bytes (its content is not specified; use any bytes), and Content-Length must equal it. Every non-2xx response body is { error, message } plus offset for offset_mismatch; message text is an example and is never matched. A test on the server side builds the context, sends the request and checks status, the headers listed and the body (ignoring message). A test on the client side feeds the response in and checks what the client does (e.g. 409 offset_mismatch: retry from body.offset). Sequences run their steps in order against one evolving context; a step with no response was cut off after interruptedAfterBytes bytes. request.bodyRaw is JSON text sent exactly as written (a JSON value cannot express duplicate keys or lone surrogate escapes); it is used instead of body. request.wrongContentType marks a request whose Content-Type is deliberately not JSON. context.transfer.owner / context.offer.owner is the device ID of the device that created or received it (absent: the requesting device). context.pairingToken.expired: true means the token is also past its 5 minutes (state used + expired is token_used). request.wrongContentType is true exactly when the Content-Type of a POST body is not application/json (ASCII case-insensitive) with no parameter or exactly charset=utf-8; PUT ignores Content-Type. context.server.createFails: the PC cannot create the file (permission, I/O error), which is 500 internal. tls[] is about the handshake, not HTTP: see the spec section Transport. In a tls[] case certificateProfile (absent = ok) says whether the leaf certificate is inside the certificate profile, failureSurfacesOn says where a refused handshake becomes visible (client_first_read: TLS 1.3 clients finish their handshake call before the server checks the client certificate, so the test must read from the connection; client_handshake: the phone's own handshake call), and optional: true marks a case the platform already guarantees.

tls.name: pc-requires-a-client-certificate
tls.note: the handshake fails: no HTTP response is sent, and so no 401. Even POST /v1/pair needs a certificate (the phone's device ID comes from it). In TLS 1.3 the client's handshake call still returns; the refusal arrives as an alert or a closed connection on its first read

tls.name: pc-accepts-an-unpaired-self-signed-certificate
tls.note: the handshake works; the HTTP layer then answers 401 unauthorized on every endpoint except POST /v1/pair

tls.name: pc-accepts-a-chain-from-an-unknown-issuer
tls.note: the issuer, dates and extensions of the client certificate are not checked; trust is the device ID, decided per request. The leaf still has to be inside the certificate profile

tls.name: pc-accepts-a-certificate-with-non-critical-extensions
tls.note: device-id.json test key 4 has a non-critical subjectKeyIdentifier: non-critical extensions are fine, and the minimal certificates of keys 1 to 3 (no extensions at all) are fine too

tls.name: pc-rejects-a-v1-client-certificate
tls.note: rustls-webpki rejects X.509 v1 and v2 certificates, even with a valid signature: a hand-written Android certificate must carry the [0] version field with the value 2

tls.name: pc-rejects-a-client-certificate-with-an-unknown-critical-extension
tls.note: the profile allows no critical extension at all; webpki refuses the ones it doesn't know

tls.name: pc-rejects-a-client-certificate-that-is-not-p256
tls.note: the leaf must carry an ECDSA P-256 key (an RSA or P-384 certificate is outside the profile)

tls.name: pc-rejects-a-replayed-certificate-without-the-private-key
tls.note: an attacker presents a paired phone's PUBLIC certificate but cannot sign: the CertificateVerify signature must be checked, or the attacker is taken for that phone

tls.name: phone-ignores-hostname-and-expiry
tls.note: only SHA-256(SPKI) against the pinned device ID is checked

tls.name: phone-rejects-a-different-key
tls.note: the phone checks the pin inside its own handshake call (its TrustManager runs before the handshake finishes)

tls.name: phone-rejects-an-invalid-certificateverify-signature
tls.note: OPTIONAL on the phone: Android's TLS stack (Conscrypt) always checks the server's CertificateVerify signature and a custom TrustManager can't turn that off, so the platform guarantees this case. An attacker can replay the PC's public certificate; only the signature proves the server holds the private key
